claims.text: Geman, Bienenstock and Doursat's 1992 analysis examines dual sources of estimation error and shows it decomposes into bias and variance: large numbers of parameter estimates raise the variance, whereas incorrect statistical models increase the bias. The authors frame this as a dilemma rather than a choice, because the two cannot be reduced independently by the same means.

source.title: Stuart Geman, Elie Bienenstock and Rene Doursat, Neural Networks and the Bias/Variance Dilemma, Neural Computation 4(1):1-58, January 1992, doi 10.1162/neco.1992.4.1.1

claims.text: The tension is stated directly: model-free approaches assume no particular geometric structure, use many parameters and exhibit high estimation variance, while controlling that variance requires model-based architectures that may increase modelling bias. Their conclusion, on the networks of that period, was that the fundamental challenges in neural modelling concern representation rather than learning as such.

source.title: Stuart Geman, Elie Bienenstock and Rene Doursat, Neural Networks and the Bias/Variance Dilemma, Neural Computation 4(1):1-58, January 1992, doi 10.1162/neco.1992.4.1.1

beats.broke: two quite different things both show up as error on unseen data — being systematically wrong, and being unstable — and a single error number adds them together without saying which you have
beats.fix: decompose the estimation error into a bias component, from the model's form being wrong, and a variance component, from the estimate moving with the sample, and treat them as separate quantities with separate remedies
beats.cost: they cannot both be reduced by the same means, since assuming less raises variance and assuming more raises bias, so past a point every reduction in one is paid for in the other
beats.interview: why more data fixes one of the two components and not the other
